title: Real-world prescribing patterns of hormonal therapy for dysmenorrhea and endometriosis in Japan: A retrospective cohort study using a nationwide claims database
content:
by Akiko Nakagomi, Tatsuya Yoshihara, Harumasa Arita, Kota Tanaka, Yosuke Ono, Osamu Yoshino

Dysmenorrhea and endometriosis impose a substantial burden on women of reproductive age. Hormonal therapy with low-dose estrogen–progestin combinations (LEP) and dienogest (DNG) is the mainstay of pharmacotherapy in Japan, yet real-world data on regimen-specific prescribing patterns remain limited. Using the Japan Medical Data Center (JMDC) Claims Database, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of women aged under 40 years who newly initiated LEP or DNG for dysmenorrhea or endometriosis between January and June 2023. Patients were followed for 12 months to assess the single-regimen prescribing pattern, regimen transition patterns, proportion of days covered (PDC), and use of continuous-administration LEP formulations. The analytic cohort comprised 16,176 patients. The most common initial regimen was ultra-low-dose fourth-generation LEP (ULD-4; 44.2%), followed by ultra-low-dose first-generation LEP (ULD-1; 20.8%), low-dose LEP (LD; 14.4%), DNG 1 mg/day (9.0%), ultra-low-dose second-generation LEP (ULD-2;4.4%), and DNG 2 mg/day (7.1%). A single-regimen prescribing pattern was observed in 84.3% of patients. This proportion was highest for DNG 2 mg/day (89.4%) and ULD-4 (87.9%), and lowest for ULD-1 (76.4%). Among patients who switched regimens, dose escalation within DNG (58.4% of DNG 1 mg/day switchers) and transition to ULD regimens from LD (80.6%) were the predominant patterns. The overall mean PDC was 64.8% ± 34.2%, with 23.6% of patients having a PDC below 30%. Approximately one in five patients (19.8%) received an LEP formulation approved for continuous administration during follow-up; among those prescribed Jemina, which can be used either continuously or cyclically, 53.4% used it continuously. These findings provide a nationwide benchmark of claims-based prescribing patterns and prescription persistence, highlighting both the high proportion of patients with a single-regimen prescribing pattern for DNG 2 mg/day and ULD-4 and the considerable proportion of patients with limited prescription coverage (PDC below 30%), a pattern that claims data alone cannot attribute to treatment discontinuation, adverse effects, or poor adherence.
